knownFor: A teacher at Rome in the middle of the second century who founded a school. By his opponents' accounts, it taught a heaven of divine powers in pairs.
shortDescription: Valentinus taught at Rome in the middle of the second century and founded a school there, a circle of students around a teacher. His opponents say it taught that heavenly powers came forth in pairs, and his own few words survive only in their books.
datesNote: No ancient source gives a year for his birth or his death. Irenaeus says he came to Rome when Hyginus was bishop there, flourished under Pius and stayed until Anicetus. Clement and Tertullian put the teachers of his kind in the reign of the emperor Antoninus, which falls in the middle of the second century. Tertullian also places him in the church at Rome under Eleutherus, a later bishop.
placeNote: Rome, where he taught and founded his school. No early source we hold says where he was born.
role: Teacher and founder of a school

keyWorks.title: Letters
keyWorks.about: known only from passages Clement of Alexandria quotes in his Stromata. One compares the heart to an inn crowded with evil spirits until the one good Father visits it. One tells of the angels' terror at Adam, the man they had formed. One, to Agathopus, says Jesus ate and drank in his own way, so great was his self-control

keyWorks.title: A sermon
keyWorks.about: known only from a passage Clement of Alexandria quotes in his Stromata, Book 4. He tells his hearers they were immortal from the beginning, and came into death to use it up, so that death might die in them

keyWorks.title: A psalm
keyWorks.about: a hymn Hippolytus of Rome quotes in his Refutation of All Heresies, Book 6, on all things hanging from spirit, the flesh from the soul and the soul from the air. The held text is damaged in two places, and the Greek and English prints differ

traces: Tertullian of Carthage says his follower Ptolemy made the divine powers into separate beings outside God, where Valentinus had held them inside God. Heracleon, Secundus and Marcus the magician each struck off paths of their own.

Hippolytus of Rome says the school split into an Italian branch, of Heracleon and Ptolemy, and an Eastern one, of Axionicus. The Italians said the body of Jesus was a body of soul, not of spirit, and the Spirit came down on it at his baptism. The Easterners said it was spiritual, because the Holy Spirit came upon Mary.

Tertullian says his students had moved so far from him that Valentinus himself was now nowhere. Yet there were still Valentinians, named after him, and only Axionicus at Antioch kept his teaching whole.
Justin Martyr, writing in his own time, already names Valentinians among groups called after the man who began each teaching.
Origen of Alexandria answers the reading of John's Gospel given by Heracleon, "the friend, as it is said, of Valentinus".
Eusebius of Caesarea says Bardaisan of Edessa first followed Valentinus, then rejected his teaching. He also says Ambrose, who held the teaching of Valentinus, was won over by Origen.
Irenaeus says those who come from Valentinus gave one of their recent writings the title "the Gospel of Truth".
For eighteen centuries his school was known almost only through the books of the men who answered it. In 1945, writings from these circles were found in Egypt.
No community survives, and none claims descent.
remembered: Irenaeus of Lyon says he adapted the principles of the Gnostic teaching, that of people who claimed a special knowledge, to his own school. Irenaeus wrote five books against what he calls knowledge falsely so called, aimed above all at Ptolemy's school, "a bud from that of Valentinus".
Irenaeus sets against the school the faith the church received from the apostles: one God, the Father Almighty, the maker of heaven and earth.

Clement of Alexandria quotes his words to argue against them. Clement says Valentinus held that some people are saved by nature, by what they were born as. Then the commandments would be useless, Clement says, and salvation would come apart from the Savior. If a different race came down to end death, "it is not Christ who has abolished death".
Tertullian calls him "the disciple of Platonism." He wrote a book Against the Valentinians, and puts Justin Martyr among those who wrote against such teachers in their own lifetime.
Hippolytus of Rome charges that he took his teaching from Pythagoras and Plato, not from the Gospels, and so should be reckoned "a Pythagorean and Platonist, not a Christian".
Hippolytus of Rome says Valentinus claimed to have seen a newborn child who told him he was the Word, a name for God's Son.
Irenaeus says Polycarp of Smyrna, at Rome when Anicetus was bishop, turned many away from Valentinus and Marcion to the church.

uncertain: Almost everything known of him comes from his opponents: Irenaeus of Lyon, Tertullian of Carthage, Clement of Alexandria and Hippolytus of Rome. His own words survive in their quotations, chiefly Clement's.

What is his and what is his school's. Irenaeus gives a short account of Valentinus himself; his long account of the powers is of Ptolemy's school. There Irenaeus reports that the school held its own members would be saved because they were spiritual by nature. Clement gives the teaching of a class saved by nature to Valentinus himself. Tertullian sets the teacher against his pupil. Hippolytus speaks of Valentinus, Heracleon, Ptolemy and the whole school together, so the teacher and his students cannot always be told apart.

Why the powers came in pairs. Hippolytus gives the school's answer: the Father was alone and was all love, and "love is not love except there may be some object of affection", so he brought forth the first pair. Hippolytus does not name the man who says it.

The fall. Irenaeus says one of the last powers broke away and fell, and from its fall came everything outside. From that line came a lesser maker who ruled what lay below. Irenaeus gives no reason for the fall here.
Tertullian places him at Rome under Bishop Eleutherus. Irenaeus places him from Hyginus to Anicetus, earlier.

The break. Of the writers near his time, only Tertullian says he broke with the church, and he gives two reasons. In one book it is anger at losing a bishopric, with ambition and a wish for revenge. In another it is a restless curiosity that spread to other believers, for which he was put out of the church at Rome more than once. Tertullian names no city for the bishopric, no year and no rival. Irenaeus tells no break.

Epiphanius of Salamis, writing long after and from hearsay, says he preached at Rome, then went to Cyprus and there left the faith. No held source gives his death. Irenaeus says only that he stayed at Rome until Anicetus.

No early source we hold says where he was born. Epiphanius says most people do not know. He passes on, as doubtful, a report that Valentinus was born on the coast of Egypt and schooled in Greek learning at Alexandria.
That he was taught by Theudas, a pupil of Paul, is his followers' claim, as Clement reports it.

The sermon. The English print gives its author as Valentinian, but its index files the passage under Valentinus, and Clement goes straight on to answer his teaching. Clement's Greek is not held. The quotation stops where the print's next clause, on dissolving the world, mixes up "we" and "yourselves".
The ending. The English print says Valentinus was "as yet nowhere". Tertullian's Latin, nusquam iam, means now nowhere, and the story follows the Latin.
The Gospel of Truth. Irenaeus says the followers of Valentinus gave a recent writing that title. No held old source says who wrote it.
The psalm. In its first word and in its verb for the soul, the held Greek is an editor's correction of a damaged manuscript. The English follows another reading.

The Eastern branch. Hippolytus names a second man in it beside Axionicus. Wendland's Greek keeps the manuscript's name for him, Ardesianes. The English prints a corrected name, and the held old sources do not say who he was.
The vision of the newborn child is a wonder, told only by Hippolytus, an opponent.

lines.text: He had hoped to become a bishop, for his talent and his gift of speech. Another man won the place by the claim his suffering for the faith gave him.

lines.text: After the break, Tertullian says, he turned to fight the truth and built his teaching on the seed of an old opinion.

timeline.witness: Clement of Alexandria, an opponent who quotes him to answer him

lines.text: In a letter, he compares the heart to an inn crowded with evil spirits. When the one good Father visits it, it is made holy and shines with light.

lines.text: In a letter, he tells how terror fell on the angels at Adam, the man they had formed, and how they quickly marred their work.

lines.text: In a letter to Agathopus, he says Jesus ate and drank in his own way, so great was his self-control that his food did not decay in him.

lines.text: In a book on the fellowship of friends, he writes that many things in common books are also found written in the church of God.

timeline.headline: His teaching, as his opponents describe it

briefReferences: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata II.20, ANF English: his letter on the heart as an inn for travelers, with holes and ruts and full of dung, its guests living filthily and taking no care of a place that belongs to others; the heart unclean and full of demons until the Father visits it. Clement quotes it to argue against him.

Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.4.3: he came to Rome under Hyginus and stayed until Anicetus. Clement, Stromata VII.17, and Tertullian, Prescription against Heretics 30: the reign of the emperor Antoninus.

Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.11.1: his own school; the first pair, Unspeakable and Silence, then Father and Truth, Word and Life, Man and Church, and more powers after them; the power that fell, from whose fall came the world and a lesser maker.

Tertullian, Against the Valentinians 4, Latin, ed. Kroymann, with the ANF English: the bishopric he hoped for, the other man's claim from his suffering for the faith, the break with the church of the true rule, ambition and the wish for revenge; the powers held inside God, and Ptolemy making them beings outside God; Valentinus now nowhere, the Valentinians still named after him, and Axionicus at Antioch keeping his teaching whole. Tertullian, Prescription against Heretics 13: the rule of faith, one God, the maker of the world.
Tertullian, Prescription against Heretics 30: put out of the church at Rome more than once, for a restless curiosity that spread to other believers.
Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 53: Tertullian of Carthage, flourishing under the emperors Severus and Caracalla.

Clement of Alexandria, Stromata IV.13: his sermon, that his hearers were immortal from the beginning and came into death to use it up; Clement's answer that he held a class saved by nature, a different race come down from above. Stromata V.1: the commandments useless, and salvation apart from the Savior's coming.
Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies VI.35: the Italian branch, Ptolemy's, and the Eastern one.

Irenaeus, Against Heresies I preface: the school of Ptolemy, a bud of Valentinus's; V preface: the fifth book of the work. Tertullian, Against the Valentinians. Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies VI.

quotationOriginals.modern: So it is with the heart, while no one gives it any thought. It is unclean, a home for many demons. But when the Father, who alone is good, visits it, it is made holy, and it shines with light.
quotationOriginals.printed: So fares it with the heart as long as there is no thought taken for it, being unclean, and the abode of many demons. But when the only good Father visits it, it is sanctified, and gleams with light.

quotationOriginals.uncertain: Clement's Greek is not held, so the modern English is rendered from the ANF English.

quotationOriginals.modern: Valentinus had hoped to be made a bishop, because he had the talent and the gift of speech for it. But another man won the place, by the claim his suffering for the faith gave him. Angry at this, he broke away from the church of the true rule.
quotationOriginals.printed: Valentinus had expected to become a bishop, because he was an able man both in genius and eloquence. Being indignant, however, that another obtained the dignity by reason of a claim which confessorship had given him, he broke with the church of the true faith.

"Suffering for the faith" renders martyrii, where the ANF has "confessorship"; "the true rule" renders authenticae regulae, where the ANF has "the true faith". The scan reads Yalentinus and aliura. Oehler's print reads Valentinus and alium, and Speraverat against the variant separauerat in Kroymann's apparatus (`tertullian_quae-supersunt-t2-polemica-lat_oehler1853.txt` lines 21632-21636; Kroymann line 9647).
